He builds AI chatbots that answer from your own documents, Python backend APIs, and computer vision and speech models. # Freelance AI chatbot and document assistant development
URL: https://shaunakchorge.github.io/Portfolio/new_portfolio/services/llm-rag-development/
Hire a freelance AI developer to build chatbots that answer from your own documents, show their sources and say "I do not know" when unsure.

I build Artificial Intelligence (AI) chatbots that answer from your own documents. Every answer shows its source. When the documents do not contain the answer, the chatbot says so instead of guessing. The method is known as RAG, short for retrieval-augmented generation. You receive a working service, a simple chat screen, tests and clear handover notes.

Deliverables: A working chatbot service with clear instructions for connecting to it (an API); Your documents prepared so the chatbot finds the right passage; Safety checks that block weak or off-topic answers; A source and a confidence label on every answer; A simple chat screen (Streamlit or React) for demos and review; Tests, setup notes and a handover walkthrough.

Good fit: Teams with policy, support or help-centre documents that need answers with sources; Founders who want to try an AI feature before hiring a full team; Products that need a chatbot or AI feature added to an existing system.

Tools: Python, FastAPI, LangChain, ChromaDB, sentence-transformers, AI model APIs (Groq, OpenAI), Pydantic, Streamlit, Docker, pytest.

Q: How do you stop the chatbot from making things up? A: With several layers, not one instruction. First the chatbot checks that the documents really contain the answer. Weak matches never reach the AI language model (LLM), the part that writes the reply. A fixed fallback sentence covers the rest. In my healthcare example, out-of-scope questions get a plain "not found" instead of a guess.

Q: Can it run on my own servers so my data stays private? A: Often, yes. At work I build on AI models hosted on the client's own servers, so no data or prompts leave the building. My personal projects use online services such as Groq. During planning we choose what fits your privacy needs, budget and answer quality.

Q: What kinds of documents can the chatbot use? A: Text-based documents such as policies, manuals, circulars and support articles. Tables and images inside documents can be harder, so we test those early. I start with a small sample of yours to check how well the chatbot finds the right passages, before we commit to the full build.

Q: Can my team maintain it after you finish? A: That is the aim. Instructions and adjustable settings live in simple config files, the code has tests, and the handover includes a walkthrough of how to add documents and tune the settings. If you want ongoing help, we can agree a maintenance period in writing.

# Document AI and data extraction
URL: https://shaunakchorge.github.io/Portfolio/new_portfolio/services/ai-document-compliance-automation/
Freelance document AI: tools that pull data from documents with source quotes, draft text with built-in checks and answer data questions.

I build tools that read PDFs, forms and reports and turn them into clean, checkable data. Every extracted fact links back to the exact quote in your document. When AI writes a draft, code checks it against the original notes. I measure accuracy on your own files, so you see real numbers before you rely on it.

Deliverables: A service that reads your documents and returns clean, structured data; Evidence links: each fact tied to the exact quote it came from; Automatic checks that reject AI-written text containing invented details; Bulk processing for spreadsheets or whole folders of documents; A scoring tool that measures accuracy on a sample of your own documents; A review screen or export (web page or spreadsheet), if you need one.

Good fit: Audit, compliance or operations teams who work through long documents by hand; Products that need AI-written text with firm limits on what it may contain; Teams that want to ask plain-language questions of a large database.

Tools: Python, FastAPI, Pydantic, PyMuPDF, Local AI models (Ollama, vLLM), RAG (answers from documents), sqlglot, React, Docker.

Q: How do you check that the extracted data is correct? A: By measuring it. I build a scoring tool that compares the output with a small set of correct answers from your documents, then fix the mistakes it finds. On one database project, running the generated queries showed that simple scoring had overstated quality.

Q: Can my documents stay on our own servers? A: Yes, and that is a common requirement. Several systems I work on use AI models hosted on the client's own servers, so documents, prompts and usage records stay on the machine. During planning we check what hardware is available, because larger models need stronger machines.

Q: How do you stop AI from adding invented details? A: With checks in code, not just instructions in a prompt. In a drafting service I built, any figure, date or owner that is not in the source note causes the draft to be rejected automatically. Reviewers can still accept, edit or reject every draft that remains.

Q: Can this connect to our existing product? A: Yes. I connected an AI drafting service to a live product built with Spring Boot and React. It runs as a separate FastAPI service with a clear agreement about the data it sends and receives, so the main product and the new service can be updated separately.

# Python backend and API development
URL: https://shaunakchorge.github.io/Portfolio/new_portfolio/services/ai-backend-fastapi-django/
Freelance Python backend developer: FastAPI and Django APIs with PostgreSQL, Docker, automated tests and logs you can use to find problems fast.

I build the behind-the-scenes software (a backend API) that lets your website, app or Artificial Intelligence (AI) feature work with your data. I write it in Python using FastAPI or Django (popular Python toolkits), store data in PostgreSQL and package it with Docker. Every service comes with automated tests and clear logs, so problems can be found quickly.

Deliverables: A backend API with documented endpoints (FastAPI or Django REST Framework); A PostgreSQL database design, with scripts to update it safely; A Docker setup so the whole system starts the same way everywhere; Automated tests for the main logic and the API (pytest); Logs, speed metrics and request traces where they help; A README, API documentation and handover notes.

Good fit: Startups that need a backend behind a website, mobile app or AI feature; Teams that need an existing service extended, tested or made easier to monitor; Projects that need background jobs, live progress updates or data sync between systems.

Tools: Python, FastAPI, Django, Django REST Framework, PostgreSQL, Pydantic, Docker, pytest, OpenTelemetry, Prometheus, Redis, Celery.

Q: Should we use FastAPI or Django? A: FastAPI suits services built around an API, including AI features. Django with Django REST Framework suits products that also need an admin area, user accounts and a built-in database layer. I use both and will recommend one after reading your requirements.

Q: Can you take over or extend an existing backend? A: Yes. Much of my professional work has been inside existing systems. I read the code before changing it, keep changes covered by tests and leave a clear decision log in the repository, so your team knows what changed and why.

Q: Can you set up background jobs and live progress updates? A: Yes. I have used Celery and Redis to move slow work away from the main API, and WebSockets to stream the progress of long-running jobs to a React web screen. Users see live status instead of waiting, and the main API stays responsive for everyone else.

Q: Will the API come with tests? A: Yes. My own backend projects ship with tests for the core logic and for each endpoint, and I take the same approach on client work. Tests make later changes safer and cheaper, and they show your team how each part is meant to behave.

# Computer vision development
URL: https://shaunakchorge.github.io/Portfolio/new_portfolio/services/computer-vision/
Freelance computer vision: tools that detect, count and classify things in photos and video with OpenCV, PyTorch and YOLOv8, with honest accuracy figures.

I build computer vision tools: software that finds, counts or sorts things in photos and video. Examples are crowd counting, spotting events in camera footage and matching faces. I tell you plainly how accurate it is, what it was tested on and where it can fail. I also deliver a small app or report your team can use.

Deliverables: A detection or classification tool for your images or video; Code that samples video frames and cleans them up first (OpenCV); A short results note that states how the tool was tested; A small Streamlit or Flask app for uploading files and viewing results; Alerts or record-keeping, such as saving to a database or sending a WhatsApp message (Twilio); A documented repository or notebook, so results can be reproduced.

Good fit: Teams that need a prototype for counting, classifying or flagging events in video; Researchers and students who need a clean, documented vision workflow; Products that want a first-pass image or video screening tool with a clear report.

Tools: Python, OpenCV, PyTorch, TensorFlow / Keras, YOLOv8, Hugging Face Transformers, Streamlit, Flask, MongoDB, Twilio.

Q: Can you train a model on my own images or video? A: Yes, for small to medium sets of images. I trained a neural network on frames from a public deepfake dataset, and I have used ready-made detectors such as Faster R-CNN, YOLOv8n and a Vision Transformer. During planning we check how much labelled data you have and whether a ready-made model is the better start.

Q: How accurate will it be? A: I will not promise a number before I see your data. I measure on data the model has not seen and state exactly how it was split. My deepfake detector reports 74.16% on a random frame-level split, and says what that does not prove.

Q: Can it work on live camera feeds? A: My monitoring prototype checks video frames on a schedule, one every three seconds for the crime module, and raises alerts. Whether your setup needs true real-time speed is something we would test during planning rather than assume, because it depends on camera quality, the number of cameras and your hardware.

Q: What about privacy for face or surveillance projects? A: Those projects need consent, clear rules on how long data is kept and legal review on your side. I raise privacy questions during planning and can build in options such as limited data retention and restricted access to stored images. The legal decisions stay with you.

# Speech, text and machine learning
URL: https://shaunakchorge.github.io/Portfolio/new_portfolio/services/speech-nlp-ml/
Freelance machine learning on audio, text and spreadsheet data: speech emotion detection, spam filters and price prediction, with honest accuracy.

I build machine learning models that learn from sound, text or spreadsheet data. Examples are detecting emotion in a voice clip, filtering spam messages and predicting prices. Each model comes with honest accuracy figures, a note on how it was tested and a small web app, so non-technical people can try it themselves.

Deliverables: Data preparation and feature extraction (librosa, TF-IDF, pandas); Model training, with a comparison against a simple baseline; A results report that states how the data was split and what that limits; A Streamlit app: upload, record or paste, then see the result; A saved model and a script that uses it; A reproducible notebook and a README.

Good fit: Teams with labelled audio, text or spreadsheet data and a clear thing to predict; Projects that need a quick, honest proof of concept before investing further; Students and researchers who want a documented, reproducible workflow.

Tools: Python, TensorFlow / Keras, librosa, scikit-learn, NLTK, pandas, NumPy, Streamlit, Hugging Face Transformers.

Q: Can you classify my own audio or text data? A: Yes, if you have labelled examples and a clear target. I have built a neural network on audio features and a spam classifier on text (TF-IDF with Naive Bayes), each with a small app around it. Before training, we check that you have enough examples of each category.

Q: How do you report accuracy? A: With the data split stated. My speech emotion model reaches 93.87% on a random 20% test split. I also say that altered copies of one clip can land on both sides, so it does not prove the model works on new speakers.

Q: Do you use ready-made models? A: When they fit. Pretrained Hugging Face models are a sensible start for many text and audio tasks. I compare against a simple baseline, so you can see what the extra complexity actually buys, and I tell you if the simple option is good enough.

Q: Can the model be offered as an API? A: Yes. A trained model can be wrapped in a FastAPI service with tests and a Docker setup, the same way I build other backends, so your apps can call it directly. Handover includes instructions for sending data to it and reading the results.

# Automation, bots and integrations
URL: https://shaunakchorge.github.io/Portfolio/new_portfolio/services/python-automation-integrations/
Freelance Python automation: web scrapers, Telegram bots and WhatsApp links through the Meta Cloud API and Twilio, with background jobs and error handling.

I automate repetitive work with Python: web scrapers that save clean tables, Telegram and WhatsApp bots, and links between your tools. Slow jobs run in the background so replies stay quick. Every automation includes error handling and logs, so you can see what happened if something goes wrong.

Deliverables: A scraper or data flow that exports to CSV, a database or an API; A Telegram or WhatsApp bot with checked, step-by-step conversations; A receiver for incoming messages (a webhook, built with FastAPI) with error handling and logs; Background jobs (Celery and Redis) for slow tasks; Alerts that hand a conversation over to a human operator; Setup notes, settings files and run instructions.

Good fit: Small businesses that answer the same customer questions on WhatsApp or Telegram; Teams that collect data from websites or exports by hand; Products that need slow AI work handled in the background without making users wait.

Tools: Python, FastAPI, Requests, BeautifulSoup, pandas, Telegram Bot API, WhatsApp Cloud API (prototype), Twilio, Celery, Redis, PostgreSQL, Supabase.

Q: Can you build a WhatsApp bot for my business? A: Yes. I worked on a WhatsApp automation platform that used the Meta Business API and Twilio, tracked each user's conversation and replied in the background. Account approval and message templates on Meta's side are part of the planning conversation.

Q: Can the bot use AI to answer? A: Yes. In a client platform I built, AI replies were queued through Redis and Celery (background job tools) so the incoming-message receiver stayed fast. Conversation flows based on what the customer wants kept complex bookings on track, and a human operator could be alerted when needed.

Q: Is it allowed to scrape a website? A: That depends on the site's terms and the data involved, and the decision is yours. Where an official API exists I suggest using it, because it is more stable. Any scraper I build keeps its request rate modest, so it does not overload the site.

Q: Where does the automation run? A: Anywhere that runs Python and Docker: your own server, a cloud machine or a managed platform. Setup instructions come with the handover, so your team can move it later. We choose the place together, based on cost, security needs and who will look after it.

# AMS AI Finding Drafting Engine
URL: https://shaunakchorge.github.io/Portfolio/new_portfolio/projects/ams-ai-finding-engine/
Case study: an AI service at Claptek that drafts audit findings with no invented facts across 27 checked drafts and about 28 times faster responses.

A standalone service at Claptek that turns short audit checklist notes into draft findings, three versions each. Code-level checks block any invented figure, date or owner.

Problem: Auditors spend hours turning terse checklist notes into well-formed findings. Simple AI drafting tends to invent figures and names.

Approach: The service finds similar past findings to use as examples, then asks an AI language model that runs on Claptek's own servers to write the draft. Hard checks in code follow: any draft containing a detail that is not in the auditor's note is rejected.

Architecture: A settings file for each bank, so one codebase serves several banks; A search step that finds similar past findings and uses them as writing examples; An AI language model on Claptek's own servers writes the title, description, recommendation and severity; Code-level checks reject any draft with a figure, date or owner that is not in the auditor's note; Three versions of every finding: short, balanced and detailed; Bulk mode: an uploaded workbook becomes a reviewable grid where each row can be accepted, edited or rejected, plus a written summary report; Connected to the client's existing audit product, which is built with Spring Boot and React.

Results: 0 invented facts across 27 checked draft versions; Time per request cut from 7.9 minutes to 16.9 seconds (about 28 times faster). I found hidden extra processing in how the system called the AI models, and accuracy stayed unchanged; 313 automated tests pass, and the code passes style and type checks; Adopted into the client's audit product the day after handover.

Role: Sole engineer at Claptek. I built it end to end: the data formats, the drafting process, the safety checks, bulk mode and the connection to the client's Java and React product.

Extensions I can build for you (not part of this build): Draft-quality scoring; Reviewer feedback loop; Speed and cost dashboards; Better search of past findings; User roles and activity history.

# Obligation Management System
URL: https://shaunakchorge.github.io/Portfolio/new_portfolio/projects/obligation-management-system/
Case study: an AI service that lists obligations from regulatory PDFs, with 97.2% of 1,266 records linked to an exact, highlightable source passage.

An Artificial Intelligence (AI) service at Claptek that reads regulatory and compliance documents and returns a structured list of obligations. Each one is linked to an exact, highlightable passage in the source PDF.

Problem: Compliance teams build obligation lists by hand from long regulatory PDFs, and the page numbers an AI model gives for them cannot be trusted.

Approach: The document is split at page boundaries. For each piece, an AI language model on Claptek's own servers extracts the obligations into fixed categories and quotes the source word for word. Code then finds that quote in the PDF and works out the page and highlight position itself.

Architecture: The document is split at page boundaries, and a merge step joins obligations that cross a page break; For each piece, an AI language model hosted on Claptek's own servers extracts obligations into fixed categories; A locator finds each word-for-word quote in the PDF (using PyMuPDF) and works out the page number and highlight position from the document itself; A side-by-side PDF preview (pdf.js) highlights the evidence for each obligation; Generation can be cancelled, which frees the model's memory and keeps the extracts already finished; A FastAPI backend, a React screen and Docker packaging.

Results: 97.2% of 1,266 production records linked to an exact, highlightable passage. The page numbers stated by the AI model had been wrong 56% of the time; 100% of records carry a word-for-word source quote; On documents held back from tuning, a controlled comparison raised recall (the share of obligations found) from 32% to 69% for Basel III banking rules and from 69% to 82% for KYC (know-your-customer) rules; Processing time for a six-document benchmark fell from 80.4 to 60.0 minutes; The same process reads permits, circulars and regulations with no domain-specific code.

Role: Primary engineer at Claptek. I wrote nearly all of the code; one colleague helped scope the early intake step.

Extensions I can build for you (not part of this build): Versioned lists and change tracking; Searchable document library; Accuracy scoring; Reviewer approval workflow; Speed dashboards.

# Core-Banking Text-to-SQL Assistant
URL: https://shaunakchorge.github.io/Portfolio/new_portfolio/projects/core-banking-text-to-sql/
Case study: an on-premise assistant that turns plain questions into bank database queries, lifting the share of accounts found from 34% to 54%.

An assistant at Claptek, running on the bank's own servers, that turns plain-language reporting questions into working Oracle database queries (SQL) over a large core-banking database. My part was the accuracy measurement and the self-correction loop.

Problem: Simple scoring said the query writer was about 93% good. Actually running its queries showed the honest figure was close to zero.

Approach: I built the measurement first: a test that runs each generated query and compares the returned rows with a known-correct query. Then I added a retry loop, limited to two passes, that shows the AI the real error and asks for a fix. The client allowed no larger model and no retraining.

Architecture: Search over a 1,628-table core-banking database to find the right tables (built by my teammate); An AI language model hosted on the bank's own servers writes the Oracle query. The query safety guard and test data were also built by my teammate; An accuracy test that runs each generated query on a real database and compares the rows with a known-correct query; A self-correction loop, limited to two passes, that feeds real query errors back to the AI; A glossary of real code values added to the prompt, so filters use values that actually exist; Fully on the bank's own servers: no data, prompt or usage record leaves the machine.

Results: Accounts found rose from 34% to 54%, and the correct share of results from 19% to 27%, with no model change and no retraining; 100% of 40 held-out test queries were valid against the live database layout; Simple scoring had suggested about 93% quality. Running the queries showed the honest number was far lower, which is why the accuracy test came first.

Role: A focused part of a two-person team at Claptek. I built the accuracy test and the self-correction loop. My teammate built the table search, the query safety guard and the test data.

Extensions I can build for you (not part of this build): Automatic accuracy checks on every change; Table search by meaning; Explained results with charts; Feedback that builds the answer key; Speed and failure tracking.

# Healthcare Policy Chatbot
URL: https://shaunakchorge.github.io/Portfolio/new_portfolio/projects/ai-rag-healthcare-assistant/
Case study: a chatbot over healthcare policy documents that cites its source and refuses out-of-scope questions instead of guessing.

A chatbot that answers questions from six made-up healthcare policy documents. It returns its source and a confidence label, and refuses out-of-scope questions instead of guessing.

Problem: Healthcare answers must come from the right document. A confident wrong answer is worse than no answer.

Approach: Three safety layers. First, the chatbot works out what the user wants. Second, weak document matches are dropped before the AI is called. Third, a strict instruction forces an exact fallback sentence when nothing relevant remains. Settings live in config files, and a chain of backup AI models keeps the service running if one is retired.

Architecture: Six made-up policy documents (appointments, discharge, health-privacy rules, insurance, refills and telehealth), cut into chunks of 500 with an overlap of 50; Meaning-based search: sentence-transformers turns text into numbers stored in ChromaDB, and the top 3 matches are used; A three-way router: booking requests go to a mock scheduling tool, small talk to a friendly persona and everything else to the document chatbot; A similarity score threshold drops weak matches before the AI is called; A strict instruction with an exact fallback sentence, returning the source passage and a confidence label; A chain of backup Groq models, prompts and settings in config files, a FastAPI backend, a Streamlit chat screen and Docker.

Results: Every answer returns its source document, the passage used and a confidence percentage; Out-of-scope questions get a fixed fallback sentence instead of a guess, because weak matches never reach the AI; The service keeps running when a hosted model is retired, with no code change; 6 quick automated tests and a Docker-packaged backend.

Role: Sole author. I wrote all of it (28 commits).

Extensions I can build for you (not part of this build): Reading real document sets; Agents that use your tools; Better search at scale; Reranking; Scored question set and stricter checks; Speed and usage dashboards.

# Scam-Catching AI Honey-Pot
URL: https://shaunakchorge.github.io/Portfolio/new_portfolio/projects/agentic-honeypot/
Case study: an AI persona that keeps scammers talking while it flags scam intent and logs payment IDs and links. Co-built with Prasanna Patil.

A counter-scam system where an AI plays an easily fooled victim, keeps scammers talking and records the UPI payment IDs, links and phone numbers they reveal. Co-built with Prasanna Patil.

Problem: A blocked scammer simply tries the next number, and nobody learns how the scam works. Keeping scammers busy with a bot protects real people for as long as it lasts and leaves a record of exactly what they ask for.

Approach: Each incoming message is scored for scam signals. A rule-based selector then changes the bot's style: passive at first, vulnerable when scam risk climbs, stalling once enough details are collected. An AI persona served by Groq writes the replies. Payment and contact details are pulled out with pattern matching and shown on a live dashboard.

Architecture: A FastAPI backend scores each message against known scam signals; A rule-based selector moves the bot through four styles: passive, engaged, vulnerable and stalling; A persona written by an AI model on Groq replies, and sees the last 10 messages; Pattern matching pulls out UPI IDs, links and phone numbers, each with a fixed confidence level per pattern type; A filter for prompt-injection attempts and a per-visitor request limiter; A live React dashboard, interactive API documentation (Scalar) and a Docker setup.

Results: The bot's style changes automatically as scam risk and collected details grow; UPI IDs, links and phone numbers are saved as structured threat information; Request limit of 1 per second per visitor, with bursts of 5; The persona sees the last 10 messages for each reply; A live dashboard shows warning signals, the current style and the details collected.

Role: Co-author with Prasanna Patil. I added the filter that blocks prompt-injection attempts (tricks that try to hijack the AI) and the request limiter, moved the AI from Gemini to Groq, rewrote the persona prompts and detail-extraction patterns, and reworked parts of the dashboard. Prasanna wrote the first version, the Docker setup and the README.

Extensions I can build for you (not part of this build): A learned scam detector with scoring; Memory and tools for the agent; Searchable conversation store; Attack-testing suite; Tracking and analytics dashboards.

# CCTV Crime and Crowd Analytics
URL: https://shaunakchorge.github.io/Portfolio/new_portfolio/projects/advanced-cctv-analytics/
Case study: a Smart India Hackathon prototype that watches one CCTV feed for crowd limits, crime types and faces. Co-built with Prasanna Patil.

A Smart India Hackathon team prototype that watches one CCTV feed three ways: crowd-limit alerts, crime labels from video frames and face recognition. Co-built with Prasanna Patil.

Problem: Public-safety teams cannot watch every camera at once. Overcrowding, violent incidents and known persons of interest slip past exactly when attention matters most.

Approach: Monitoring is split into three independent modules. One counts crowds, one labels video frames for crime types and one recognises faces. Each saves evidence frames to MongoDB and sends alerts through Twilio WhatsApp.

Architecture: Crowd module: OpenCV removes the background to find moving people and counts them as they cross virtual lines. Past a set limit it beeps and sends a WhatsApp alert; Crime module: a pre-trained Vision Transformer, fine-tuned on the UCF-Crime dataset (14 crime categories), labels one frame every 3 seconds; Face module: Haar cascades find faces and LBPH recognition matches them, with a small tool to enrol persons of interest; Evidence frames and labels stored in MongoDB; Flask pages to review the latest detections; Twilio WhatsApp API for alerts.

Results: Three independent monitoring modules on one camera feed; 14 crime categories labelled from frames sampled every 3 seconds; Evidence frames and labels saved to MongoDB, with Flask pages to view the latest detections; Won the internal round of the Smart India Hackathon at college.

Role: Member of the Smart India Hackathon team. Co-built with Prasanna Patil.

Extensions I can build for you (not part of this build): Modern people detector and tracker; Live camera stream input; Accuracy testing on your footage; Alert dashboard and rules; Privacy controls.

# Speech Emotion Recognition
URL: https://shaunakchorge.github.io/Portfolio/new_portfolio/projects/speech-emotion-recognition/
Case study: a neural network that labels seven emotions in speech, 93.87% on a random test split, with live microphone input and a web app.

A neural network (a 1-D CNN) that labels seven emotions in speech clips. It was trained on four public datasets and comes with live microphone input and a web dashboard.

Problem: Emotion lives in tone, pitch and energy, not in the words, so a text-based model is the wrong tool.

Approach: Four datasets are merged and each clip is altered to create more training examples. Audio features are extracted with librosa, then a five-block neural network learns from them. The result is served through notebooks and a Streamlit dashboard.

Architecture: Four public datasets (RAVDESS, CREMA-D, TESS and SAVEE) merged into 12,162 clips; Each clip altered four ways with noise and pitch changes, giving 48,648 training samples; librosa audio features: zero-crossing rate, energy and MFCCs, 2,376 numbers per sample; A five-block 1-D neural network with steps to prevent overfitting, 7.19 million parameters; A notebook for live microphone input; A Streamlit dashboard: upload or record, then see class probabilities and waveform and spectrogram views.

Results: Recognises seven emotions: angry, disgust, fear, happy, neutral, sad and surprise; 93.87% accuracy and a weighted F1 score of 0.94 on a random 20% test split; Per-emotion F1 scores between 0.92 and 0.97; Caveat: altered copies of one clip can land on both sides of the split, so the result does not prove it works on new speakers; Live microphone detection in a notebook and in the Streamlit dashboard.

Role: I adapted a public training recipe from Kaggle, retrained and tested it on four datasets, then wrote the live-input notebook and the Streamlit dashboard.

Extensions I can build for you (not part of this build): Testing on voices it has never heard; Pretrained speech model comparison; Prediction API; Live browser microphone.

# DeepFake Video Detection
URL: https://shaunakchorge.github.io/Portfolio/new_portfolio/projects/deepfake-video-detection/
Case study: a neural network that scores each video frame as real or fake, with a web app and PDF report. 74.16% on a random frame split.

A college team project in which a small neural network scores every frame of an uploaded video as real or fake, with a web app, a confidence chart and a downloadable PDF report. Co-built with Prasanna Patil and a classmate.

Problem: Face-swap videos are hard to spot by eye, so reviewers need a quick, explainable first check.

Approach: The first ten frames of each Celeb-DF video are resized to 224 by 224 pixels and used to train a small neural network with augmentation. A six-page Streamlit app then scores every frame of an uploaded video and explains confidence bands.

Architecture: The first ten frames of each Celeb-DF video, resized to 224 by 224 pixels and varied slightly to add training variety; A small three-block neural network (CNN) trained on 7,856 frames; Frame scores averaged into a Real or Fake verdict; A six-page Streamlit app with a frame-by-frame confidence chart and an explanation of confidence bands; PDF report export with ReportLab.

Results: 74.16% test accuracy on a random frame-level split. The team's own report lists this as room for improvement; An end-to-end flow from upload and frame extraction to scoring, chart and PDF report; A 31-page project report with requirements, risk table and literature survey.

Role: Member of a three-person college team. The repository is published from my account.

Extensions I can build for you (not part of this build): A stronger model that watches across frames; Fairer testing by video; Face finding and cropping; Batch scoring API; Visual explanations.

# Traceable AI Backend
URL: https://shaunakchorge.github.io/Portfolio/new_portfolio/projects/observable-ai-backend/
Case study: an AI-routed backend with request IDs, metrics and traces. A slow step fell from about 15 seconds to under 50 milliseconds on made-up data.

A FastAPI service where an AI picks one of three business actions for each question. A request ID follows every call through logs, metrics and traces (viewed in Jaeger), so a slow or failing call can be explained from the outside.

Problem: An AI endpoint can return a success code and still be slow, degraded or quietly switching to another model. You only find out when users complain.

Approach: One request ID is stamped on every log line and trace step of a request. Simple, hand-written metrics count requests, AI response time, tokens used and model fallbacks. Three Groq models are chained with a time limit each and a clear "degraded" flag, so a silent fallback becomes visible.

Architecture: An /ask endpoint where an AI picks one of three business actions (look up tickets, create a ticket or run a sales report) and then summarises the result; A chain of three Groq models, each with a time limit and an explicit "degraded" flag; One request ID on every log line and trace step; Hand-written Prometheus metrics for requests, AI response time, tokens and model fallbacks; OpenTelemetry traces viewed in Jaeger; A simple keyword router, so the service runs with no API key or internet; A Docker Compose setup that starts the app, Jaeger and Prometheus together.

Results: A deliberately slow lookup (a join over 60,000 made-up tickets) was found in a trace. Its step fell from about 15 seconds to under 50 milliseconds once indexed; 10 automated tests that need no key or internet; Silent model fallbacks are visible through the degraded flag and a fallback counter.

Role: Sole author. Built with AI assistance (Claude Code); design decisions and the options I rejected are logged in the repository.

Extensions I can build for you (not part of this build): Dashboards and alerts; Caching and request limits; Sign-in and usage quotas; Routing accuracy test set; Cloud deployment with automatic tests.

# Freelance AI developer FAQ
URL: https://shaunakchorge.github.io/Portfolio/new_portfolio/faq/
Answers about hiring Shaunak Chorge: cost, how to start, time zone, NDAs, ownership, fixing existing projects and support after delivery.

Shaunak Chorge takes select freelance Artificial Intelligence (AI) and backend projects alongside his full-time job as an AI Engineer at Claptek Pvt Ltd. He works remotely from Mumbai (IST), starts from a short written brief and agrees the scope before writing any code. Each project is priced individually, and you receive tested code with clear notes.

Q: Do you take on freelance projects? A: Yes. I take select freelance AI and backend projects alongside my full-time job as an AI Engineer at Claptek Pvt Ltd. I keep the number small so every client gets proper attention, and I am upfront about scope and timelines before we agree to work together.

Q: What kinds of projects do you build? A: I build AI chatbots that answer from your documents, tools that read and extract data from documents, and Python backend APIs. I also build computer vision, speech and text models, and automation such as web scrapers and Telegram or WhatsApp bots. Each area has its own page under Services, with examples of real work.

Q: Can you fix or extend my existing project? A: Yes. Most of my professional work has been inside software that already existed. I added an AI drafting service to a live audit product and sped up the core matching code during an internship. I read the code before changing it, keep changes tested and leave notes explaining each decision.

Q: How do we start? A: Send a short brief through the contact form or by email: what you want to build, roughly when you need it and anything I should know. I reply with my view on feasibility and a proposed scope. We agree on both before I write any code.

Q: What does a project look like from start to finish? A: Four steps. First we agree on the problem and how success will be measured. Then I build a small working prototype on your data. Next I add tests and safety checks. Finally I hand over notes and a walkthrough. You see working software early and get short written updates along the way.

Q: How long will my project take? A: It depends on the size of the project. After reading your brief, I give a written estimate for each step. A small prototype is much quicker than a full product. I would rather give you an honest range than promise a date I cannot keep.

Q: Which tools do you use? A: I work mostly in Python. For web services I use FastAPI and PostgreSQL, packaged with Docker. For AI I use services such as Groq and OpenAI, plus LangChain and ChromaDB for chatbots that search your documents. For vision and speech I use OpenCV, PyTorch and TensorFlow. The full list is on the About page.

Q: Can the AI run on our own servers instead of an online service? A: Yes. At work I build on AI language models (LLMs) hosted on the client's own servers, for systems where no data, prompt or usage record may leave the building. My personal projects use online services such as Groq. We choose based on your privacy needs, cost and answer quality.

Q: What time zone do you work in? A: I am based in Mumbai, India, and work in Indian Standard Time (IST, UTC+5:30). I work remotely, using written updates and shared code reviews. We can agree meeting times that overlap with your working day. A past remote internship taught me how to keep distant teams in sync.

Q: How much does it cost? A: I do not publish a price list, because projects vary too much. After reading your brief, I suggest either a fixed price for a clearly defined scope, or hourly billing for open-ended work. The price and the terms are agreed in writing before I start.

Q: Do you sign an NDA? A: Yes. I am happy to sign a reasonable mutual NDA (a confidentiality agreement) before we discuss private details. I do not reuse client data or code in other projects, and I only name a client or show their work in my portfolio with written approval.

Q: Who owns the code and the final work? A: The ownership and licence terms are written into our agreement before work begins. The usual arrangement is that you own what you pay for. My freelance work is kept separate from my full-time job and never uses my employer's code or data.

Q: What happens after you hand the project over? A: Handover includes a README (a how-to guide), setup instructions, tests and a walkthrough, so your team can run and extend the work. A bug-fix period and ongoing maintenance can be agreed as part of the scope, and I will write down exactly what is covered.
